Songs with weather in the title.Waterloo: ABBA's 1974 Eurovision winner. Waterloo is a Belgian battle, not a storm.
Songs with weather in the title.Respect: Aretha Franklin's 1967 hit. No weather at all.
Songs with weather in the title.Yellow: Coldplay's 2000 hit about starlight, with no weather in the name.
Songs with weather in the title.Under the Sea: From Disney's The Little Mermaid, it won the 1989 Oscar for Best Original Song. Sea, not sky.

Tennis shots.Forehand: The shot struck on your dominant side, usually the first one learned. Pros hit it with topspin so heavy the ball can spin over 3,000 times a minute.
Tennis shots.Backhand: Struck across the body from the non-dominant side. Players can use one hand or two, and the two-handed version was popularized by Jimmy Connors and Chris Evert.
Tennis shots.Serve: The only shot a player fully controls, and elite men serve beyond 130 mph. Aces are often the quickest route to a point.
Tennis shots.Volley: Hitting the ball before it bounces, usually near the net. Doubles specialists live on it, because short reaction times reward quick hands.
Tennis shots.Lob: A shot lofted over an opponent at the net. It is a clever way to turn a net rusher's aggression against them and can win a point.
Tennis shots.Smash: The overhead swing that punishes a weak lob. It resembles a serve in motion, and a pro's smash can pass 100 mph.
Tennis shots.Drop shot: A delicate shot that barely clears the net and dies on the second bounce. Played well, it drags a baseline player forward, which wrecks their rhythm.
Tennis shots.Topspin: A forward-rotating spin that makes the ball dip and kick up after bouncing. Rafael Nadal built much of his dominance on extreme topspin.
Tennis shots.Half volley: Hitting the ball right after it bounces, with no time for a full swing. It is a tough shot, and pros often play it from a low crouch.
Tennis shots.Passing shot: A winner hit past a player at the net, often down the line or crosswise. Attackers hate it, and it gives baseliners an equalizer.
Tennis shots.Moonball: A very high, looping, deep shot meant to push an opponent off balance. Despite sneering from purists, it has won plenty of matches.
Tennis shots.Tweener: A hit made between the legs while running back to a lob. Guillermo Vilas and later Federer and others made the shot a crowd favorite.
Tennis shots.Putt: A golf stroke rolled along the green. In tennis, the nearest equivalent is a gentle drop shot, though no one uses a putter on court.
Tennis shots.Chip: A golf shot that pops onto the green. Tennis has a 'chip' too, but that's the sliced return, so it can seem to fit; here it means the golf version.
Tennis shots.Bunt: A baseball tap with a held bat, so the ball dribbles in the infield. Tennis has no such ploy, and trying it with a racket would not end well.
Tennis shots.Dunk: A basketball slam through the hoop. Tennis players do not leap and force the ball down through a ring, though a smash may feel similar.
Tennis shots.Header: A soccer move in which the head strikes the ball. Tennis players hit with the racket only, and that rule keeps the sport tidy.
Tennis shots.Jab: A quick straight punch in boxing. Tennis players do jab at a volley, but that's a description of a motion, not a named shot.
Tennis shots.Googly: A cricket delivery that looks like a leg-spin ball but turns the other way. Tennis has no such delivery, though spin serves can fool a returner.
Tennis shots.Spike: A hard downward volleyball hit. In tennis the sharp-looking shot is a smash, and spikes appear only on track shoes.
Tennis shots.Layup: A close-range basketball shot that is gently banked in off the board. Tennis doesn't have a layup, though a soft putaway volley is similar.
Tennis shots.Uppercut: A boxing punch that rises from below. A tennis stroke that lifts the ball, topspin, has a similar motion, but the name belongs to boxing.
Tennis shots.Slap shot: A hockey shot with a big wind-up that can top 100 mph. It rhymes with tennis power, but the sport's racket never earns this name.
Tennis shots.Bank shot: A basketball shot, or pool shot, where the ball bounces off a surface first. Tennis rules don't use a backboard, so the idea doesn't fit.

Monsters of Greek myth.Medusa: A Gorgon with snakes for hair whose gaze turned people to stone. She was killed by Perseus, and the winged horse Pegasus sprang from her blood.
Monsters of Greek myth.Minotaur: Half-man, half-bull, kept in Crete's Labyrinth built by Daedalus. Theseus killed it with Ariadne's help.
Monsters of Greek myth.Cyclops: A giant with one eye. The best-known, Polyphemus, was tricked by Odysseus, who called himself "Nobody."
Monsters of Greek myth.Hydra: A many-headed serpent of Lerna, killed by Heracles with help from his nephew Iolaus, who seared the severed necks.
Monsters of Greek myth.Cerberus: The three-headed hound who guards the gates of the underworld, keeping the dead in. Heracles dragged it to the surface as his final labor.
Monsters of Greek myth.Chimera: A fire-breathing hybrid of lion, goat and snake. Today the word also means an organism built from genetically different cells.
Monsters of Greek myth.Scylla: A six-headed sea monster who snatched sailors from ships, on one side of a narrow strait. The other side held Charybdis.
Monsters of Greek myth.Charybdis: A giant whirlpool that swallowed ships three times a day. "Between Scylla and Charybdis" still means choosing between two evils.
Monsters of Greek myth.Harpy: A winged female spirit with a woman's face who snatched food and people away. They tormented the blind king Phineus.
Monsters of Greek myth.Typhon: The deadliest monster of Greek myth, father of many others, who challenged Zeus himself. Zeus buried him under a volcano, Etna.
Monsters of Greek myth.Siren: Creatures whose songs lured sailors to wreck on rocks. Odysseus had his crew plug their ears and tied himself to the mast.
Monsters of Greek myth.Kraken: A giant sea monster from Scandinavian legend, not Greek. It likely grew from sightings of huge squid.
Monsters of Greek myth.Fenrir: The giant wolf of Norse myth, fated to devour Odin at Ragnarok. He is Norse, not Greek.
Monsters of Greek myth.Jormungandr: The Midgard Serpent of Norse myth, so long it circles the whole world. Thor's great enemy, and nothing to do with the Greeks.
Monsters of Greek myth.Grendel: The man-eating monster slain by Beowulf in the Old English poem. It's a Scandinavian-set tale.
Monsters of Greek myth.Banshee: A wailing spirit of Irish folklore whose cry warns of an approaching death. Celtic, not Greek.
Monsters of Greek myth.Vampire: A trap: the blood-drinking undead come from Eastern European folklore. Greek myth had related spirits like the lamia, but not vampires.
Monsters of Greek myth.Yeti: The "abominable snowman" of Himalayan legend. Fits the monster idea, but Tibetan and Nepali folklore, not Greek.
Monsters of Greek myth.Bigfoot: A hairy ape-like creature of North American folklore, also called Sasquatch. Widely reported, never proven.
Monsters of Greek myth.Golem: A clay figure brought to life in Jewish folklore, most famously in Prague. Not from Greece.
Monsters of Greek myth.Wendigo: A cannibal spirit from Algonquian folklore linked with winter and starvation. Native American in origin.
Monsters of Greek myth.Troll: A creature of Scandinavian folklore, often living under bridges or in mountains. Not from Greek myth.
Monsters of Greek myth.Mummy: The wrapped corpse is an Egyptian practice, so mummy monsters come from Egypt-inspired fiction, not Greek myth.
Monsters of Greek myth.Chupacabra: A "goat-sucker" first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. A very modern legend, not ancient myth.

Famous queens.Cleopatra: Egypt's last ruling Ptolemaic queen was Greek-descended but learned Egyptian, and the first of her family to do so.
Famous queens.Elizabeth I: She reigned 44 years, never married, and saw off the Spanish Armada in 1588.
Famous queens.Victoria: She was queen of the United Kingdom and, from 1876, Empress of India, for 63 years.
Famous queens.Boudica: This Iceni queen led a revolt against Rome in AD 60 or 61 and burned London.
Famous queens.Nefertiti: Queen of Egypt as the wife of Akhenaten. Her painted bust in Berlin is among the most famous ancient portraits.
Famous queens.Isabella of Castile: She sponsored Columbus in 1492 and with Ferdinand united Spain's kingdoms.
Famous queens.Marie Antoinette: Austrian-born queen of France, guillotined in 1793. There is no proof she ever said let them eat cake.
Famous queens.Catherine the Great: A German-born princess, she seized Russia's throne in a coup against her husband and ruled for 34 years.
Famous queens.Mary Queen of Scots: She became queen at six days old and was held by Elizabeth I for 19 years before being executed in 1587.
Famous queens.Eleanor of Aquitaine: She was queen of both France and England, and mother of Richard the Lionheart and King John.
Famous queens.Anne Boleyn: The second wife of Henry VIII, executed in 1536. She was mother of Elizabeth I.
Famous queens.Zenobia: Queen of Palmyra, who broke away from Rome around AD 270 and took Egypt before being defeated.
Famous queens.Joan of Arc: A peasant girl who led armies and was made a saint, but she was never a queen, since she helped crown Charles VII.
Famous queens.Florence Nightingale: A nurse and statistician, not a monarch. She was nicknamed the Lady with the Lamp.
Famous queens.Marie Curie: She won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry. A scientist and a pioneer, not a queen.
Famous queens.Amelia Earhart: She was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, and vanished in 1937 over the Pacific. Not royalty.
Famous queens.Pocahontas: The daughter of a Powhatan chief, not a queen, though she was often called a princess by the English.
Famous queens.Mona Lisa: Leonardo's painting, not a monarch. She was likely a Florentine merchant's wife, Lisa Gherardini.
Famous queens.Rosa Parks: Her 1955 refusal to give up a bus seat helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott. Not a queen.
Famous queens.Helen Keller: She was deaf and blind, and became a famous author and activist. Not royalty.
Famous queens.Ada Lovelace: A countess and early programmer, daughter of Lord Byron. A countess, not a queen.
Famous queens.Jane Austen: A novelist who wrote Pride and Prejudice and Emma, ruling no kingdom but the bookshelf.
Famous queens.Frida Kahlo: A Mexican painter known for her self-portraits. Art royalty, but not a queen.
Famous queens.Sacagawea: The Shoshone woman guided Lewis and Clark across the American West, carrying her infant son. She was no queen.

Things usually made of rubber.Rubber band: Stephen Perry patented the rubber band in 1845 in England, and they can last for years before the rubber dries.
Things usually made of rubber.Eraser: Before rubber, people rubbed out pencil with bread, which is why rubber took the name 'rubber' in Britain.
Things usually made of rubber.Rubber duck: Rubber ducks were reportedly first made in the late 1800s, and in 1992, a spill at sea sent thousands across the ocean.
Things usually made of rubber.Balloon: Latex balloons are made from natural rubber, and the air slowly leaks through it, so they deflate even when tied.
Things usually made of rubber.Tire: Tires are mostly synthetic rubber blended with natural rubber, and carbon black, which makes them strong and black.
Things usually made of rubber.Hot water bottle: Rubber bottles have been used since the 1800s, and the stopper is screwed tight so it won't leak.
Things usually made of rubber.Rubber gloves: Rubber gloves were first used in surgery in 1889, when a nurse developed a rash from harsh chemicals.
Things usually made of rubber.Wellington boots: Named after the Duke of Wellington, they were once leather riding boots before waterproof rubber took over.
Things usually made of rubber.Bath plug: A rubber stopper's elasticity lets it make a tight seal against the drain.
Things usually made of rubber.Bouncy ball: The Super Ball, invented in 1964 from a synthetic rubber compound, could bounce nearly as high as it was dropped.
Things usually made of rubber.Hockey puck: An ice hockey puck is made of vulcanized rubber, and teams freeze pucks before games so they slide with less bounce.
Things usually made of rubber.Pencil: A pencil is wood and graphite, though many carry a small rubber eraser at the tip.
Things usually made of rubber.Spoon: A spoon is hard material, not rubber, though silicone spoons are used in cooking.
Things usually made of rubber.Glass: Glass is hard and brittle, nearly the opposite of rubber, which is stretchy and soft.
Things usually made of rubber.Book: Books are paper and ink, though the old binding glue was made from animal hide.
Things usually made of rubber.Brick: Brick is baked clay, hard and heavy, not stretchy at all.
Things usually made of rubber.Coin: Coins are metal, and no coin you'll see is made of rubber.
Things usually made of rubber.Mirror: A mirror is glass plus a reflective metal layer, so there's no rubber at all.
Things usually made of rubber.Paper clip: Paper clips are bent steel wire, usually zinc-coated to prevent rust.
Things usually made of rubber.Towel: Towels are woven cotton loops that soak up water, nothing like waterproof rubber.
Things usually made of rubber.Feather: A feather is made of keratin, and it's light and soft but not stretchy.
Things usually made of rubber.Teacup: Teacups are porcelain or ceramic, fired clay with a glaze to hold the hot tea.
Things usually made of rubber.Matchbox: Matchboxes are cardboard with a strip of sandpaper-like material for striking the match.
Things usually made of rubber.Lightbulb: A lightbulb is glass and metal, with no rubber, though old wires were insulated with it.

Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Coat hanger: Wire coat hangers date to around 1903, and the bent-wire design is credited to Albert Parkhouse, though the story is often retold.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Dresses: Dresses hang better than they fold, because folds can leave stubborn creases in the fabric.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Shirts: Shirts are best hung on a hanger to stay crisp, while knits stretch if hung.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Coats: Coats are bulky, and a wardrobe's tall space was designed to let long garments hang freely.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Shoes: Shoes are often stored in a wardrobe's base, and cedar inserts help them stay fresh.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Suits: Suits keep their shape best on wide shouldered hangers.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Belts: Belts roll up or hang on hooks, and leather keeps its shape better if not folded.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Shoe rack: A shoe rack keeps pairs organized so they don't scuff each other.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Ties: Ties should be hung or rolled to avoid creases and damage to the silk.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Hat box: A hat box protects shape, and its round form dates back to when everyone wore hats.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Mothballs: Mothballs contain chemicals that give off fumes to repel clothes moths, and they have a strong smell.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Jackets: Jackets hang best with their shoulders fitted to the hanger to avoid creases in the sleeves.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Toaster: A toaster belongs on the kitchen counter, where it can be plugged in safely.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Saucepan: A saucepan lives in a kitchen cupboard, not among clothes.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Toothbrush: A toothbrush belongs in the bathroom, and bacteria would build up in a wardrobe.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Shower gel: Shower gel is for the bathroom, where it won't stain clothes.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Cutlery: Cutlery goes in a kitchen drawer, so it doesn't clank among coats.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Frying pan: A frying pan is kitchen gear, and it would leave grease on your clothes.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Kettle: A kettle sits on the kitchen counter and is plugged in, never kept in a wardrobe.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Microwave: A microwave needs a power socket and a kitchen, not a clothes cupboard.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Dish soap: Dish soap lives by the sink, and it would stain fabrics.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Dinner plates: Dinner plates stay in the kitchen cupboard, away from clothes.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Fridge magnets: Fridge magnets belong on the fridge, and they'd have no use in a wardrobe.
Things you'd find in a wardrobe.Spice jars: Spice jars go in the kitchen, where the smell won't cling to clothes.

Cereal grains.Wheat: Wheat feeds a huge share of humanity and is grown on more land than any other crop. It was among the first plants farmers domesticated.
Cereal grains.Corn: Maize was bred from a scraggly Mexican grass called teosinte roughly 9,000 years ago. Its cobs are far larger than its wild ancestor's.
Cereal grains.Barley: Among the first cultivated grains, it is a main ingredient of beer and whisky. Malting turns its starches into fermentable sugars.
Cereal grains.Rice: Rice feeds over half the world's people. It is usually grown in flooded paddies, which keep weeds down.
Cereal grains.Oats: Long thought of as horse feed, oats are rich in a soluble fibre called beta-glucan, which is linked to lower cholesterol.
Cereal grains.Rye: Tough and cold-hardy, rye thrives where wheat struggles, which is why dark rye bread is so common in northern and eastern Europe.
Cereal grains.Sorghum: A drought-tolerant staple in Africa and India, it can be popped like popcorn and is also made into syrup and gluten-free flour.
Cereal grains.Millet: Small-seeded millets were grown in China some 10,000 years ago. They're famously resilient in dry, poor soils.
Cereal grains.Spelt: An ancient wheat relative that Romans prized. It has a tough husk that protects the grain and survives long storage.
Cereal grains.Teff: This tiny Ethiopian grain is ground into flour for injera flatbread. Its seeds are so small that a single wheat grain equals about 150 of them.
Cereal grains.Triticale: A human-made hybrid of wheat and rye, first bred in the late 1800s. Its name blends the Latin names Triticum and Secale.
Cereal grains.Soybeans: A legume, not a cereal grain. Soybeans are protein-rich and are crushed into oil and animal feed, as well as tofu.
Cereal grains.Lentils: These are pulses, the seeds of a legume. They were among the earliest foods farmed, with remains from the Middle East thousands of years old.
Cereal grains.Chickpeas: Legumes rather than true grains. Their cooking water, aquafaba, whips up like egg whites and is used in vegan meringues.
Cereal grains.Flax: A seed crop, used for linseed oil and linen cloth. Linen fabric comes from its stem fibres and was wrapped around Egyptian mummies.
Cereal grains.Sunflower: A oilseed, not a cereal. Young flower heads track the sun across the sky, a behaviour called heliotropism.
Cereal grains.Peanut: Not a nut or a grain: it's a legume whose pods ripen underground. The plant pushes its flowers into the soil after pollination.
Cereal grains.Potato: A starchy tuber, not a grain. Originating in the Andes, it was long one of the most important foods in the cold climates of Europe.
Cereal grains.Cotton: A fibre crop, grown for the fluff around its seeds rather than for food. Its seed is pressed for cooking oil, though.
Cereal grains.Canola: Its name stands for 'Canadian oil, low acid'. It was bred from rapeseed to remove a bitter compound, making the oil fit for cooking.
Cereal grains.Sugar beet: A root crop. In temperate regions it supplies a large share of the world's sugar, which cane would otherwise provide.
Cereal grains.Hemp: A cannabis variety grown for strong fibres and edible seeds. It's a broadleaf plant, not a cereal grass.
Cereal grains.Coffee: Coffee 'beans' are actually seeds inside a fruit called a cherry. It's a shrub, which puts it far from the cereal family.
Cereal grains.Cocoa: Chocolate comes from seeds of a tropical tree, the cacao, whose pods grow straight out of the trunk. Not a grain.

Military vehicles.Tank: The name was a cover story: in 1915 British workers were told the new armored machines were water tanks, to hide their purpose.
Military vehicles.Humvee: Built to replace the Jeep, its official name is HMMWV, and its wide stance inspired the civilian Hummer.
Military vehicles.Fighter jet: Many modern fighters are deliberately unstable, so flight computers adjust the control surfaces constantly to keep them in the air.
Military vehicles.Submarine: Nuclear submarines can stay submerged for months; the real limit is how much food the crew can carry.
Military vehicles.Aircraft carrier: A US supercarrier is a floating airfield, and its steam catapults fling a jet from standstill to flying speed in about two seconds.
Military vehicles.Destroyer: The name began with torpedo-boat destroyers of the 1890s, built to hunt small torpedo boats before growing into general warships.
Military vehicles.Frigate: Frigates were the fast scouts of the sailing-ship era; today the name covers mid-sized escort warships.
Military vehicles.Black Hawk: Named after a Sauk war leader, this UH-60 helicopter has served the US Army since the late 1970s and carries about eleven troops.
Military vehicles.Armored car: Wheeled instead of tracked, armored cars are faster and quieter on roads than tanks, which is why armies use them for scouting.
Military vehicles.Stealth bomber: The B-2 Spirit costs well over a billion dollars each, and its flying-wing shape deflects radar instead of reflecting it back.
Military vehicles.Ice cream truck: Entirely civilian, and older than motor vans: street vendors sold ice cream from hand carts long before trucks took over.
Military vehicles.Double-decker bus: London's red buses look civilian, yet in 1914 hundreds were shipped to France to carry troops to the Western Front.
Military vehicles.Gondola: Venetian gondolas are always painted black, a habit tied to old laws against showy spending.
Military vehicles.Limousine: Armored presidential limos exist, but the limousine itself is a luxury car, named after France's Limousin region.
Military vehicles.Tuk-tuk: Named for the putter of its small engine, this three-wheeled taxi is everyday transport in Thailand and beyond, not a military machine.
Military vehicles.Rickshaw: The word comes from Japanese jinrikisha, meaning human-powered vehicle; it is civilian transport through and through.
Military vehicles.Zamboni: Frank Zamboni built his first ice-resurfacing machine in California in 1949; it is a rink machine, not a military one.
Military vehicles.Segway: Civilian, though police patrol on them; Segway's owner Jimi Heselden died in 2010 when his own Segway went off a cliff.
Military vehicles.Cable car: San Francisco's cable cars are the last manually operated system of their kind, hauled along by a constantly moving underground cable.
Military vehicles.Tram: A civilian streetcar on rails; Melbourne runs one of the largest tram networks in the world.
Military vehicles.Monster truck: Strictly entertainment: Bigfoot, built in 1975, is widely seen as the first monster truck.
Military vehicles.Go-kart: Art Ingels built the first go-kart in California in 1956, powered by a lawnmower engine; it is strictly for fun.
Military vehicles.Hearse: The word comes from a Latin term for a harrow, first used for a candle frame set over a coffin.
Military vehicles.Pedalo: A pedal-powered pleasure boat for lakes and seaside; however swan-shaped, it is leisure craft rather than warship.

Ways to connect to the internet.Wi-Fi: The name is a pun on 'hi-fi' and doesn't stand for anything, despite the myth of 'wireless fidelity'. It started in 1997 as the 802.11 standard.
Ways to connect to the internet.Ethernet: Invented at Xerox PARC in 1973 by Bob Metcalfe, it's named after the discredited 'luminiferous ether' once believed to carry light.
Ways to connect to the internet.Dial-up: Modems screeched at about 56 kilobits per second, using the same line as your phone, so a call would knock you offline.
Ways to connect to the internet.DSL: Digital Subscriber Line squeezes internet signals over copper phone wires at frequencies above those used for voice, so you can talk and browse.
Ways to connect to the internet.Cable: It uses the same coaxial cable that carries TV, and it shares neighborhood bandwidth, so speeds can drop when everyone streams at once.
Ways to connect to the internet.Fiber: Data travels as pulses of light through glass strands thinner than a hair, at speeds that can top a gigabit per second.
Ways to connect to the internet.Satellite: Geostationary dishes sit about 35,800 kilometers up, so signals take about half a second to go there and back.
Ways to connect to the internet.5G: This cellular network can be many times faster than 4G, and it spawned persistent conspiracy theories that scientific evidence doesn't support.
Ways to connect to the internet.4G LTE: The 'LTE' stands for Long Term Evolution, and it made mobile video streaming feasible as the standard from around 2010.
Ways to connect to the internet.Mobile hotspot: Your phone can share its cellular connection over Wi-Fi, which turns it into a tiny router for a laptop.
Ways to connect to the internet.Starlink: SpaceX's satellite constellation has launched thousands of low-orbit satellites, giving internet to remote places like ships and polar bases.
Ways to connect to the internet.HDMI: A trap: it carries video and audio from a device to a screen, but it doesn't connect you to the internet.
Ways to connect to the internet.VGA: It sends an analog picture to a monitor, a 1987 IBM standard that's still around, but it can't connect you to the web.
Ways to connect to the internet.Morse code: A trap: Samuel Morse's dots and dashes carried telegraph messages in the 1800s, long before the internet, and cannot get you online.
Ways to connect to the internet.Walkie-talkie: A short-range radio for voice calls, so it's no link to the internet. Motorola developed the first ones for soldiers in World War II.
Ways to connect to the internet.Telegraph: It sent electric messages in the 1800s, and a transatlantic cable was laid in 1858, but it isn't an internet connection.
Ways to connect to the internet.Smoke signal: Smoke signals are among the oldest long-distance messages, and they predate the internet by thousands of years.
Ways to connect to the internet.Carrier pigeon: In 2009 a South African pigeon beat a broadband line at moving data in a famous race, but it's no real connection.
Ways to connect to the internet.Megaphone: A cone that amplifies a voice, so it won't link you to the web. Cheerleaders and protesters have made good use of them for generations.
Ways to connect to the internet.Semaphore: Flag signaling uses arm positions to spell out letters, a way to talk but not to get online.
Ways to connect to the internet.Tin can phone: It uses a taut string to carry vibrations, so it's a toy telephone, not an internet connection.
Ways to connect to the internet.DisplayPort: A trap: DisplayPort sends video from a computer to a monitor, so it moves pictures, not internet data.
Ways to connect to the internet.Headphone jack: A trap: the classic 3.5 mm jack carries analog audio signals, so it can't connect a device to the internet.
Ways to connect to the internet.Aux cable: A trap: a plain analog audio lead that lets a phone play sound through a car stereo, and it can't bring you online.

Star Wars droids.R2-D2: Sound designer Ben Burtt built his beeps from electronic noises and his own voice, and R2 is the only character in all nine Skywalker-saga films.
Star Wars droids.C-3PO: Anthony Daniels wore the gold suit, which was so uncomfortable that he reportedly could not sit down in it.
Star Wars droids.BB-8: The rolling droid in The Force Awakens was a practical puppet, with its head held on by magnets over the sphere.
Star Wars droids.K-2SO: Alan Tudyk voiced this reprogrammed Imperial droid in Rogue One, and he performed it on set in a motion-capture suit on stilts.
Star Wars droids.IG-88: This assassin droid appears briefly in The Empire Strikes Back among the bounty hunters Vader summoned.
Star Wars droids.Chopper: The grumpy astromech of Star Wars Rebels is known as C1-10P and is noted for his temper, and he was designed with mismatched parts.
Star Wars droids.BD-1: The little droid of Jedi: Fallen Order rides on Cal Kestis's back, and its gentle beeps made it a fan favorite.
Star Wars droids.IG-11: Taika Waititi voiced this bounty-hunter droid in The Mandalorian, and its sacrifice in the first season made fans emotional.
Star Wars droids.L3-37: Lando's sassy co-pilot in Solo was a droid who fought for droid rights, and her brain was merged with the Millennium Falcon.
Star Wars droids.Droideka: Also called destroyer droids, they roll into a ball and then unfold, and they shield themselves from blaster fire.
Star Wars droids.Battle droid: The Separatist army's soldiers in the prequels were laughably easy to defeat, and their lines were comic relief.
Star Wars droids.R5-D4: This red droid's bad motivator blew up when Luke's uncle bought it, and so R2-D2 got the chance to join the family.
Star Wars droids.Gonk droid: These walking power generators get their name from the repeated sound they make, which sound designer Ben Burtt turned into a catchphrase.
Star Wars droids.WALL-E: This Pixar trash-compacting robot from 2008 spends most of his film saying very few words, but he is not from a galaxy far away.
Star Wars droids.EVE: The sleek probe robot from WALL-E is a Pixar creation, so she is not a Star Wars droid.
Star Wars droids.Bender: Futurama's drinking, cigar-smoking robot is a creation of Matt Groening, not from a galaxy far, far away.
Star Wars droids.Baymax: Disney's inflatable health robot from Big Hero 6 was inspired by soft robotics research at Carnegie Mellon, and is not a droid.
Star Wars droids.Johnny 5: This robot from the 1986 film Short Circuit is not a droid, although he also became sentient after a lightning strike.
Star Wars droids.Robby the Robot: He debuted in the 1956 film Forbidden Planet and later appeared in many shows, but he is not from Star Wars.
Star Wars droids.K-9: The robot dog of Doctor Who is a fixture of that show, so he is not a Star Wars droid.
Star Wars droids.Rosie: The Jetsons' robot maid belongs to the cartoon family, not a galaxy far away.
Star Wars droids.Optimus Prime: Peter Cullen voiced the Autobot leader, and while he is a robot, he is a Transformer, not a droid.
Star Wars droids.Iron Giant: Brad Bird's 1999 film gave this robot a gentle heart, and he is from a children's book by Ted Hughes.
Star Wars droids.Bumblebee: This yellow Autobot is a Transformer, which is why he does not appear on the list of droids.

Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Odysseus: Odysseus is the clever hero who takes ten years to get home after the Trojan War, using the trick of the Trojan Horse.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Penelope: Penelope waits twenty years for Odysseus, holding off suitors by weaving a shroud by day and unpicking it each night.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Telemachus: Telemachus, Odysseus's son, sets out to look for news of his missing father, and later helps him fight the suitors.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Athena: Athena, goddess of wisdom, is Odysseus's patron, who guides him and disguises him as a beggar when he returns.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Polyphemus: Polyphemus, the Cyclops, is tricked when Odysseus says his name is Nobody, so his cries for help are ignored.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Circe: Circe is the sorceress who turns Odysseus's men into pigs, until he, protected by the herb moly, forces her to reverse the spell.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Calypso: Calypso is the nymph who keeps Odysseus on her island, Ogygia, for seven years, until the gods order his release.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Poseidon: Poseidon is the sea god who is angry at Odysseus for blinding his son, Polyphemus, and delays his voyage.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Argos: Argos is Odysseus's old hound, the only one to recognize him in disguise, and then he dies.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Scylla: Scylla is the six-headed sea monster, who snatches sailors from ships passing through the strait.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Charybdis: Charybdis is the whirlpool across from Scylla, behind the phrase between Scylla and Charybdis.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Nausicaa: Nausicaa is the Phaeacian princess who finds Odysseus washed up on the shore and helps him.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Eumaeus: Eumaeus is the loyal swineherd who shelters the disguised Odysseus and helps him retake his home.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Beowulf: Beowulf is the hero of an Old English poem, set in Scandinavia, who fights Grendel and has no link to Homer.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Gilgamesh: Gilgamesh is the Mesopotamian king of an epic, a story that predates Homer by well over a thousand years.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Dido: Dido is the queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid, where she falls in love with Aeneas, not in the Odyssey.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Aeneas: Aeneas fights at Troy in the Iliad, but his own story is Virgil's Aeneid, written in Latin centuries later.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Romulus: Romulus is the legendary founder of Rome, said to have killed his brother Remus, a Roman legend, not Greek epic.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Gawain: Gawain is King Arthur's nephew and a knight famed for Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, not for Homer.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Icarus: Icarus is the boy who flew too near the sun on wax wings, a Greek myth but not from the Odyssey.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Pandora: Pandora, who opened the jar of evils, belongs to Hesiod's poems, not Homer's Odyssey.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Sinbad: Sinbad is a sailor from the Arabian Nights, whose voyages echo Odysseus's, but he's from a separate tradition.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Spartacus: Spartacus was a real gladiator who led a slave revolt against Rome around 73 BC, long after Homer.
Characters in Homer's Odyssey.Thor: Thor is the Norse god of thunder, wielding the hammer Mjolnir, and has no place in Greek epic.

French painters.Claude Monet: He painted over 250 water lily canvases at his garden in Giverny, and gave Impressionism its name.
French painters.Renoir: He kept painting in old age, with brushes strapped to hands crippled by arthritis, and favored cheerful scenes.
French painters.Edgar Degas: Famed for dancers, he disliked being called an Impressionist, and he worked mostly indoors.
French painters.Édouard Manet: His 1863 Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe and Olympia scandalized Paris, and he influenced the Impressionists.
French painters.Paul Cézanne: Picasso reportedly called him "the father of us all", and his apples and Mont Sainte-Victoire paved the way to Cubism.
French painters.Paul Gauguin: He left a banking job to paint and sailed to Tahiti in 1891, seeking a world untouched by Europe.
French painters.Henri Matisse: The founder of Fauvism, he made cut-paper art from his bed in old age, when he couldn't stand to paint.
French painters.Georges Seurat: His pointillist A Sunday on La Grande Jatte took two years and thousands of tiny dots of color.
French painters.Eugène Delacroix: His Liberty Leading the People, from 1830, commemorates the July Revolution, and has become a French symbol.
French painters.Gustave Courbet: The realist was jailed in 1871 for his supposed role in toppling the Vendôme Column in Paris.
French painters.Toulouse-Lautrec: He chronicled Montmartre and the Moulin Rouge in posters, and stood about 1.5 meters tall.
French painters.Ingres: In French, "violon d'Ingres" means a hobby, since he was a skilled violinist as well as a painter.
French painters.Nicolas Poussin: A seventeenth-century master of classical painting, who worked mostly in Rome, but is thought of as French.
French painters.Watteau: The Rococo painter of fêtes galantes, he died at only 36 and left elegant scenes of party-going aristocrats.
French painters.Van Gogh: Dutch, though he painted in Arles and Auvers-sur-Oise in France, and so isn't counted as a French painter.
French painters.Pablo Picasso: Spanish, and he lived in France for most of his adult life, but remained a Spanish citizen.
French painters.Modigliani: Italian, who made his name in Paris with long-necked portraits, so he doesn't count as French.
French painters.Mary Cassatt: An American who spent most of her career in Paris, exhibiting with the Impressionists, but she wasn't French.
French painters.Salvador Dalí: A Spanish Surrealist who spent time in Paris in the 1920s and 30s, but he remained Spanish.
French painters.René Magritte: A Belgian Surrealist, who lived in Paris for a few years in the 1920s, but he remained Belgian.
French painters.Rubens: A Flemish master who painted a famous cycle for Marie de' Medici in Paris, but he wasn't French.
French painters.Gustav Klimt: An Austrian Symbolist, famed for gold leaf and The Kiss, so he isn't counted as a French painter.
French painters.Edvard Munch: A Norwegian, though he lived in Paris and Berlin for years, so he is not counted as French.
French painters.J. M. W. Turner: A British landscape master, who painted the Thames and Venice, so he isn't a French painter.

Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Red hood: Charles Perrault gave her a red hood in 1697; it's the detail that stuck, while earlier oral versions had no named garment.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Basket: In the Grimms' version it holds cake and wine for the sick grandmother, a gift meant to make her stronger.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Grandmother: The Grimms' wolf swallows her whole and she's rescued alive; in Perrault's version she stays eaten.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Wolf: In Perrault's original, the wolf wins and eats the girl, a warning about trusting charming strangers, with no rescue.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Huntsman: He appears only in the Grimms' 1812 version, cutting open the wolf to free the victims; Perrault's story has no rescuer.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Forest: The Grimms' mother warns her not to stray from the path, a rule that the girl breaks right in the wolf's presence.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Cake: Cake and wine in the Grimms, galette and butter in Perrault: the treats change with whichever local food each teller knew.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Pot of butter: Perrault's 1697 version has a galette and a little pot of butter, simple country gifts for a sick relative.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Flowers: In the Grimms' version the wolf talks her into gathering flowers, giving him time to reach the grandmother's house first.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Nightcap: The wolf dons the grandmother's nightcap, the disguise that sets up the famous "what big eyes you have" exchange.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Bed: In Perrault's ending, the girl undresses and climbs into bed beside the wolf, who then eats her.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Glass slipper: Cinderella's, from a different story; in Perrault's 1697 version, her shoe is glass.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Poisoned apple: Snow White's. The queen's poisoned apple is the Grimms' invention; it doesn't appear in Red Riding Hood.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Magic beans: Jack and the Beanstalk's beans; Red Riding Hood has no magic at all.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Spinning wheel: Sleeping Beauty's, from a different Perrault tale, which Perrault published in the same collection.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Pumpkin carriage: Cinderella's coach is magic, made from a pumpkin by her fairy godmother in Perrault's 1697 text.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Seven dwarfs: Snow White's seven helpers belong to a different story, first published by the Grimms in 1812.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Pea: Andersen's "The Princess and the Pea" (1835) has a real princess feeling one pea under twenty mattresses.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Frog prince: In the Grimms' Frog Prince, the princess throws the frog against the wall to break the spell; the kiss came later.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Gingerbread house: Hansel and Gretel's witch lives in a candy house; here the wolf's lair is the grandmother's cottage.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Three bears: Goldilocks meets three bears in a woodland cottage, a tale first printed by Robert Southey in 1837.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Straw house: The first of three little pigs builds one, and a wolf blows it down: a different wolf story.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Mermaid tail: Andersen's Little Mermaid (1837) trades her voice for legs, a Danish tale far from any forest path.
Things in Little Red Riding Hood.Golden goose: In the Grimms' tale, anyone touching the golden goose gets stuck to it, a parade of villagers in a line.

Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Pygmalion: Shaw's 1913 play inspired My Fair Lady; he insisted Eliza would not marry Higgins, an ending the musical changes.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Saint Joan: Written in 1923 soon after Joan's canonization in 1920, it helped Shaw win the Nobel Prize in 1925.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Arms and the Man: A 1894 anti-war comedy whose Swiss mercenary carries chocolate instead of bullets; it inspired The Chocolate Soldier operetta.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Major Barbara: A 1905 play where a Salvation Army major confronts her father, a wealthy arms maker.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Man and Superman: This 1903 comedy contains a long "Don Juan in Hell" dream scene often performed on its own.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Candida: An 1894 play where a minister's wife must choose between her husband and a young poet.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Heartbreak House: Written during WWI, it's set in a house shaped like a ship, and shows Shaw's debt to Chekhov.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.The Doctor's Dilemma: A 1906 play in which a doctor must decide which patient to save with a limited supply of a new cure; Shaw distrusted the medical profession.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Caesar and Cleopatra: In Shaw's 1898 comedy Caesar is a middle-aged and wry general while Cleopatra is a teenager, quite unlike Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Back to Methuselah: This 1921 cycle of five plays spans the Garden of Eden to the year 31,920 AD.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Misalliance: A 1910 comedy set in a country house where an aeroplane crashes into the greenhouse.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.An Ideal Husband: Oscar Wilde wrote this 1895 comedy about a politician's blackmailed secret.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Salome: Wilde wrote it in French in 1891; it was banned in England, and Strauss later made an opera.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Juno and the Paycock: Seán O'Casey's 1924 tragicomedy is set in Dublin tenements; a different Irish dramatist.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Private Lives: Noël Coward wrote this 1930 comedy of ex-spouses honeymooning in adjoining rooms.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Hay Fever: Noël Coward's 1925 comedy is about a theatrical family that bewilders its weekend guests.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Blithe Spirit: Noël Coward's 1941 comedy features a ghostly first wife, written in just five days.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Look Back in Anger: John Osborne's 1956 play launched the "angry young men" movement.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.An Inspector Calls: J. B. Priestley's 1945 play features a mysterious inspector at a dinner party.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Waiting for Godot: Samuel Beckett's 1953 play has two men waiting for someone who never arrives.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Antony and Cleopatra: Shakespeare, not Shaw, wrote this tragedy; Shaw's Caesar and Cleopatra covers the earlier Roman era.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.The Seagull: Chekhov's 1896 play, famous for its failed premiere; the Moscow Art Theatre made it a hit in 1898.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Hedda Gabler: Ibsen wrote this 1890 play whose heroine shoots herself at the end.
Plays by George Bernard Shaw.Uncle Vanya: Another Chekhov play, written in the 1890s, about a country estate in Russia.

Things that come in pairs.Socks: Socks come in pairs, and some people think the dryer eats one, though most go missing in the laundry.
Things that come in pairs.Shoes: Left and right shoes were not made different until the early 1800s; before that, they were identical.
Things that come in pairs.Gloves: Gloves come in pairs, and a left glove can be turned inside out to fit the right hand, if it is thin enough.
Things that come in pairs.Earrings: Earrings are among the oldest jewelry, and 'ötzi the Iceman' had stretched earlobes some 5,000 years ago.
Things that come in pairs.Chopsticks: Chopsticks have been used in China for at least 3,000 years, and they are always a pair.
Things that come in pairs.Skis: Skis are used in pairs, and the oldest known one, found in Russia, is thought to be some 8,000 years old.
Things that come in pairs.Twins: Roughly 1 in 30 births in many countries is a twin pair, and the pair is among the few that always come two at a time.
Things that come in pairs.Mittens: Mittens keep fingers warmer than gloves because the fingers share heat, and they come in pairs.
Things that come in pairs.Ice skates: Skates come in pairs, and the oldest known pair is made from animal bones, around 3000 BC.
Things that come in pairs.Drumsticks: Drumsticks are sold in pairs, and many drummers have a favorite hickory model.
Things that come in pairs.Maracas: Maracas are traditionally played in pairs, and the name comes from the Tupi-Guarani language.
Things that come in pairs.Hat: A hat is worn singly, and one head needs just one.
Things that come in pairs.Scarf: A scarf is worn alone, as one long piece.
Things that come in pairs.Necklace: A necklace is a single item, and people don't wear two matching ones.
Things that come in pairs.Belt: A belt is a single strap, and you wear just one.
Things that come in pairs.Triplets: Triplets are three, not two, and natural ones are rare, about 1 birth in several thousand.
Things that come in pairs.Wristwatch: A watch is worn on one wrist, typically alone.
Things that come in pairs.Tie: A necktie is single, and the modern form traces to Croatian soldiers in the 17th century.
Things that come in pairs.Umbrella: An umbrella is single, and one covers a person in the rain.
Things that come in pairs.Fork: A fork is a single utensil, and it was once considered scandalous in Europe.
Things that come in pairs.Backpack: A backpack is one bag, even though it has two straps.
Things that come in pairs.Crown: A crown is single, so a monarch wears just one at a time.
Things that come in pairs.Snowboard: A snowboard is one board, unlike skis, so riders use only one.
Things that come in pairs.Skateboard: A skateboard is one board with four wheels, not a pair.

Things that bounce when dropped.Basketball: A regulation basketball bounces back to about 60 percent of its drop height, which is checked before official games.
Things that bounce when dropped.Tennis ball: A tennis ball is pressurized rubber, and bounces less once the air leaks out over weeks.
Things that bounce when dropped.Bouncy ball: The Super Ball, invented in 1964 by chemist Norman Stingley, can bounce back to nearly its drop height.
Things that bounce when dropped.Soccer ball: A modern soccer ball is a pressurized bladder with panels, and it should rebound about 60 percent of drop height.
Things that bounce when dropped.Golf ball: Golf balls are made with rubbery cores that spring back, and they bounce high from hard surfaces.
Things that bounce when dropped.Ping-pong ball: A table tennis ball weighs just 2.7 grams, and it bounces well on a hard table.
Things that bounce when dropped.Beach ball: A beach ball is inflated with air, so it bounces, though lightly, and drifts with the wind.
Things that bounce when dropped.Volleyball: A volleyball is a pressurized bladder, and it rebounds when dropped, which is why it can be played on the court.
Things that bounce when dropped.Racquetball: A racquetball is hollow rubber made to bounce off walls, and the game takes advantage of it.
Things that bounce when dropped.Dodgeball: Dodgeballs are made of rubber foam, and they bounce so they can be thrown at players.
Things that bounce when dropped.Kickball: Kickball uses a large rubber ball, which bounces when dropped or kicked.
Things that bounce when dropped.Egg: An egg shatters because its shell is thin and brittle, though a raw egg can survive drops onto soft surfaces.
Things that bounce when dropped.Water balloon: It bursts on impact because the thin latex can't hold the sudden pressure.
Things that bounce when dropped.Tomato: A tomato splats when dropped because its soft flesh absorbs the impact, with no spring.
Things that bounce when dropped.Glass vase: Glass is brittle, and it shatters under impact, because it can't deform to absorb energy.
Things that bounce when dropped.Brick: A brick is rigid and nearly inelastic, so it thuds rather than bounces.
Things that bounce when dropped.Lump of clay: Clay deforms and keeps its dent, so it absorbs the energy without bouncing back.
Things that bounce when dropped.Beanbag: The loose beans inside shift and absorb impact, and so it doesn't bounce.
Things that bounce when dropped.Feather: A feather is so light and has so much air resistance that it floats down, with no bounce.
Things that bounce when dropped.Pancake: A pancake is soft and floppy, so it lands with a slap and not a bounce.
Things that bounce when dropped.Sandwich: A sandwich is soft and has no spring, so it lands with no bounce, though butter side down is a famed myth.
Things that bounce when dropped.Wet sponge: A wet sponge soaks up the energy, and it lands with a splat, not a bounce.
Things that bounce when dropped.Pie: A pie is soft and crumbly, so it splatters and doesn't bounce.
Things that bounce when dropped.Hacky sack: A footbag is filled with pellets that shift, so it drops dead rather than bouncing, by design.

Shades of green.Emerald: Emerald is green beryl, coloured by chromium and vanadium; flawless stones are far rarer and often pricier than diamonds.
Shades of green.Olive green: The shade of unripe olives is also the classic military colour, because it blends with vegetation and dull earth.
Shades of green.Lime green: A bright yellow-green named for the citrus fruit; it is a common choice for high-visibility safety vests.
Shades of green.Mint: Mint green is named for the leaf of the plant, whose cool pale shade became a staple of 1950s kitchen appliances.
Shades of green.Forest green: It is a deep, dark green that is also an official colour in crayon sets and sports uniforms around the world.
Shades of green.Sage: Sage green is a soft gray-green named for the herb's dusty leaves, and it has become a popular interior-paint shade.
Shades of green.Jade: Jade's name can describe two stones, jadeite and nephrite, and the best jadeite has long been valued in China above gold.
Shades of green.Kelly green: A vivid, saturated green, linked with Irish heritage, that is the traditional colour of Boston Celtics jerseys.
Shades of green.Hunter green: This very dark green was used to camouflage hunters and is still popular for sporting jackets and billiard tables.
Shades of green.Moss green: Mosses lack true roots and absorb water through their leaves, and their soft muted green is the origin of this shade.
Shades of green.Shamrock green: Named after Ireland's three-leaved clover emblem, which the legend says St. Patrick used to teach the Trinity.
Shades of green.Crimson: Crimson was originally made from the kermes insect, and it is a deep red that has no green in it at all.
Shades of green.Navy: Navy is a dark blue taken from British naval uniforms, which makes it a clear non-green on any colour chart.
Shades of green.Mauve: Mauve is a pale purple, and the first dye made in a lab, from coal tar by William Perkin in 1856.
Shades of green.Ochre: Ochre is a yellow-brown earth pigment, used on cave walls tens of thousands of years ago, not a green.
Shades of green.Scarlet: A bright red, and its name once described a fine cloth before it described a colour at all.
Shades of green.Cobalt: Cobalt blue is a deep, strong blue, and the pigment has been used in ceramics and glass for centuries.
Shades of green.Burgundy: A purplish red named for the wine region in France, so it is far from green.
Shades of green.Lavender: This pale purple is named after a fragrant plant, which has green leaves but flowers of the shade itself.
Shades of green.Amber: Amber is fossilised tree resin, often golden orange, and sometimes holds ancient insects trapped inside.
Shades of green.Magenta: Named after an 1859 battle in Italy, magenta is not a spectral colour, since your brain invents it from red and blue.
Shades of green.Salmon: The pinkish-orange shade comes from the fish's flesh, whose colour is from carotenoids they get from eating krill.
Shades of green.Coral: The pinkish-orange named for marine coral, though the animals themselves come in many colours, including greens.
Shades of green.Taupe: A brownish gray from the French word for "mole", the small burrowing mammal.

Things usually stored in a freezer.Ice cream: Ice cream is about half air by volume, a quantity the industry calls overrun.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Ice cubes: Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold, the Mpemba effect, and scientists still debate why.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Popsicle: The Popsicle was invented by 11-year-old Frank Epperson in 1905, who left soda with a stirring stick outside overnight.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Frozen peas: Frozen peas are blanched and frozen within hours of picking, so they often hold more nutrients than so-called fresh peas that travel for days.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Fish sticks: Fish sticks were popularized in the 1950s by Birds Eye, and are called fish fingers in Britain.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Frozen pizza: Frozen pizza took off in the 1950s and 60s, once home freezers got big enough for more than ice trays.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Ice pack: Most gel ice packs are mostly water thickened with a polymer, so they can be refrozen again and again.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Tater tots: Tater tots were created in 1953 by the founders of Ore-Ida to use up leftover potato scraps.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Sorbet: Sorbet comes from the Turkish and Arabic words for a cold sweet drink, and it contains no dairy.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Eggo waffles: Eggo waffles launched in 1953 under the name Froffles, until the brand was renamed for the eggy flavor.
Things usually stored in a freezer.TV dinner: Swanson's first TV dinner in 1953 was turkey, created to use up an enormous leftover surplus of Thanksgiving birds.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Bananas: Bananas are usually kept on the counter, because cold turns their skins black; frozen peeled ones, though, are a smoothie staple.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Potatoes: Storing raw potatoes in the cold converts their starch to sugar, which turns them sweet and brown when fried.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Onions: Onions keep best in a cool, dry, airy spot, and freezing leaves them mushy once they thaw.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Honey: Honey rarely freezes solid in a home freezer because of its sugar content; it just gets thick.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Peanut butter: Peanut butter stays spreadable even when cold, thanks to its oils, and belongs in the pantry.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Cereal: Cornflakes were invented by accident in 1894 when cooked wheat was left out and went stale.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Canned soup: Canning, heating food in a sealed container, was invented around 1800 in France in response to a call for better rations for Napoleon's army.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Dry rice: White rice can last decades in airtight storage, though brown rice's oils turn it rancid much sooner.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Dry pasta: Dry pasta, dehydrated durum wheat dough, keeps for years in the cupboard.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Olive oil: Olive oil turns cloudy and partly solid in the fridge, which is harmless but a nuisance.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Tomatoes: Cold fridges make tomatoes mealy and destroy flavor compounds, so keep them on the counter.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Crackers: Crackers are baked low in moisture and belong in a dry cupboard, since humidity makes them go limp.
Things usually stored in a freezer.Garlic: Garlic keeps best in a cool, dry, ventilated spot, and refrigeration tends to make it sprout.

Things made of frozen water.Igloo: Igloos are built from compacted snow blocks, and body heat inside can keep them far warmer than the air outside.
Things made of frozen water.Snowman: A snowman appears in a medieval manuscript from around 1380, so building them is an old pastime.
Things made of frozen water.Icicle: Icicles grow as meltwater runs down and refreezes in a thin film, forming a hollow tip that thickens over time.
Things made of frozen water.Glacier: Glaciers are slow rivers of ice that carved fjords and U-shaped valleys, and hold most of Earth's fresh water.
Things made of frozen water.Iceberg: Roughly nine-tenths of an iceberg's volume floats below the waterline, which is why the tip fools sailors.
Things made of frozen water.Hailstone: Hailstones grow in layers as storm updrafts toss them; the heaviest recorded in the US weighed almost two pounds.
Things made of frozen water.Ice sculpture: Sculptors favor crystal-clear ice, frozen slowly with moving water so it has no cloudy air bubbles.
Things made of frozen water.Snowflake: Every snowflake is a single ice crystal with six-fold symmetry, a result of how water molecules bond.
Things made of frozen water.Frost: Frost forms when water vapor turns directly into ice on a cold surface, skipping the liquid stage.
Things made of frozen water.Snow fort: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator, so a snow fort blocks wind and holds warmth.
Things made of frozen water.Sleet: Sleet is rain that freezes into pellets on the way down; in the UK, the word means a rain and snow mix.
Things made of frozen water.Dry ice: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide at about minus 78 degrees Celsius, and it turns straight into gas instead of melting.
Things made of frozen water.Sand castle: Sand castles need damp sand to hold together, so they are sand and water, with no ice.
Things made of frozen water.Cotton candy: Spun-sugar cotton candy was popularized in 1897 by a dentist, William Morrison, and a confectioner.
Things made of frozen water.Fog: Fog is a cloud at ground level made of liquid droplets; only freezing fog turns to ice, and only on contact.
Things made of frozen water.Steam: Steam is invisible water vapor; the white plume you actually see is tiny liquid droplets.
Things made of frozen water.Rain: Raindrops are liquid, and larger ones flatten into a shape like a hamburger bun rather than a teardrop.
Things made of frozen water.Dew: Dew is vapor condensing into liquid on cool surfaces overnight; if it's cold enough, it becomes frost instead.
Things made of frozen water.Salt crystal: Salt crystals are cubes of sodium chloride, and while salt can melt ice, it is not frozen water.
Things made of frozen water.Quartz: The word crystal comes from the Greek for ice, because ancients believed quartz was ice frozen forever.
Things made of frozen water.Sugar cube: Sugar cubes were invented in the 1840s, and are crystals of sucrose, not ice despite the glassy look.
Things made of frozen water.Glass: Glass is melted sand cooled into an amorphous solid; it looks icy but contains no water.
Things made of frozen water.Styrofoam: Styrofoam-type foam is mostly air trapped in plastic, which is why it floats and keeps drinks cold.
Things made of frozen water.Meringue: Meringue looks like snow but is egg-white foam stabilized by sugar and baked dry at low heat.

Things in a supermarket.Checkout: Checkout lanes use a conveyor belt and scanner, and the first barcode scan took place in 1974, on a pack of chewing gum.
Things in a supermarket.Trolley: The word "trolley" in Britain means the cart; in America it can mean a tram.
Things in a supermarket.Aisle: Supermarkets often put milk and eggs at the back so shoppers walk the whole store; the word aisle once meant a wing of a church.
Things in a supermarket.Shopping cart: Sylvan Goldman invented the shopping cart in 1937, and shoppers at first refused to use it.
Things in a supermarket.Barcode scanner: The first item ever scanned at a checkout was a pack of Wrigley's gum, in Troy, Ohio, in 1974.
Things in a supermarket.Freezer: Freezers owe their existence to Clarence Birdseye, who developed quick-freezing after seeing Inuit freeze fish in the Arctic.
Things in a supermarket.Deli counter: The word "deli" is short for delicatessen, from a German word meaning delicacies.
Things in a supermarket.Self-checkout: Self-checkout machines started appearing in the 1980s and now handle a large share of purchases.
Things in a supermarket.Price tag: Price tags appeared in the 1800s; before that, prices were often haggled for.
Things in a supermarket.Conveyor belt: The belt at the checkout is a descendant of belts first used in factories and mines.
Things in a supermarket.Shelf: Shelves at eye level are the prime spots, and brands often pay supermarkets for the best ones.
Things in a supermarket.Runway: A runway is where aircraft take off; supermarkets have aisles, though some stores do have catwalk-like displays.
Things in a supermarket.Gangplank: A gangplank is the board linking a ship to the shore; supermarkets use automatic doors instead.
Things in a supermarket.Pulpit: A pulpit is a raised stand in a church; a supermarket has no such thing.
Things in a supermarket.Altar: An altar is a church fixture; the nearest supermarket thing is a promotional display at the end of an aisle.
Things in a supermarket.Throne: A throne is for kings and queens; supermarkets use trolleys instead.
Things in a supermarket.Haystack: A haystack is found in a farm, and a supermarket sells packaged hay for pets, but not in stacks.
Things in a supermarket.Diving board: Diving boards belong at swimming pools; supermarkets have no pool, but plenty of frozen sections.
Things in a supermarket.Trapeze: A trapeze belongs to the circus and has no business among the cereal boxes.
Things in a supermarket.Bunk bed: Bunk beds are for sleeping, and supermarkets don't have beds, though some open around the clock.
Things in a supermarket.Cockpit: A cockpit is the pilot's cabin; the nearest supermarket equivalent is the checkout operator's seat.
Things in a supermarket.Fire pole: A fire pole is a way for firefighters to slide down quickly at a fire station, not a supermarket fixture.
Things in a supermarket.Hay bale: A hay bale is typically found at a farm, though supermarkets in rural areas sell garden bales.
Things in a supermarket.Hammock: A hammock was invented by the people of Central and South America, and is for lazing, not shopping.

Natural fibres.Cotton: Cotton is soft thanks to the cellulose fibre in the seedpod, and a single pound of it can be spun into miles of thread.
Natural fibres.Linen: Linen comes from the flax plant, and is among the oldest textiles; Egyptians wrapped mummies in it.
Natural fibres.Wool: Wool is the fleece of sheep, and the fibre's natural crimp traps air, which is why it insulates even when damp.
Natural fibres.Silk: Silk comes from the cocoon of the silkworm, and a single cocoon can be unwound as a thread up to a kilometre long.
Natural fibres.Hemp: Hemp is one of the oldest cultivated fibre crops, and it was used for sails and ropes, from which the word canvas derives.
Natural fibres.Jute: Jute is a plant fibre from Bengal, and it's used for burlap sacks and rope, and it is called the golden fibre.
Natural fibres.Cashmere: Cashmere is the soft undercoat of Kashmir goats, and the name derives from the region of Kashmir.
Natural fibres.Mohair: Mohair is the silky wool of the Angora goat, and it is notably lustrous and resilient.
Natural fibres.Alpaca: Alpaca fibre is warmer than sheep's wool, and is also hypoallergenic because it contains no lanolin.
Natural fibres.Angora: Angora wool comes from the Angora rabbit, which is sheared or combed, and is named for Ankara, Turkey.
Natural fibres.Flax: Flax is the plant that makes linen, and its seeds, called linseed, are also crushed for oil.
Natural fibres.Sisal: Sisal is a stiff fibre from an agave plant, often used for rope, twine and dartboards.
Natural fibres.Merino: Merino is a breed of sheep with very fine wool, and it is widely used in outdoor clothing.
Natural fibres.Polyester: A trap: polyester is made from petroleum, so it is synthetic, and the most-used fibre in clothing.
Natural fibres.Nylon: Nylon, introduced by DuPont in 1938, was the first fully synthetic fibre, and became famous for stockings.
Natural fibres.Acrylic: Acrylic is a synthetic fibre developed to imitate wool, and is made from petroleum-based chemicals.
Natural fibres.Spandex: Spandex is synthetic and can stretch to over five times its length; the name is an anagram of 'expands'.
Natural fibres.Rayon: A trap: rayon comes from plant cellulose, yet it is processed chemically, so it is semi-synthetic, not natural.
Natural fibres.Lycra: Lycra is a brand of spandex, a synthetic stretch fibre, and was invented in 1958.
Natural fibres.Kevlar: Kevlar is a synthetic aramid fibre invented by Stephanie Kwolek, and is used in bulletproof vests as it is five times stronger than steel.
Natural fibres.Vinyl: Vinyl is a plastic, made from PVC, and obviously synthetic; it is used for records and flooring too.
Natural fibres.Microfiber: Microfiber is made from ultra-fine synthetic strands, usually polyester or nylon, so it's not natural.
Natural fibres.Gore-Tex: Gore-Tex is a waterproof, breathable membrane made from a plastic, so it's entirely synthetic.
Natural fibres.Neoprene: Neoprene is a synthetic rubber, used in wetsuits, and it was invented in the 1930s.

Things in a traditional nativity scene.Mary: Often painted in blue; ultramarine, made from ground lapis lazuli, was once among the costliest pigments, reserved for her robes.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Joseph: A carpenter, and in Matthew's gospel an angel tells him in a dream to take Mary as his wife.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Baby Jesus: Many households keep the figure hidden until Christmas Eve or midnight, so the scene is not complete until he arrives.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Manger: A feeding trough for animals. The word comes from French manger, to eat.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Shepherds: In Luke's gospel they are the first to hear the news, announced by angels, while watching their flocks by night.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Wise men: The Bible never says how many. The traditional three comes from the three gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Angel: In Luke, Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a child, and an angel chorus then sings to the shepherds.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Star: The Star of Bethlehem guides the wise men in Matthew's gospel. Astronomers still debate whether it was a comet or a planetary conjunction.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Donkey: Not mentioned in the gospels' birth accounts. The animals came from later tradition, first appearing in a medieval-era text.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Ox: With the donkey, inspired by Isaiah: the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's crib.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Sheep: Present because shepherds were watching their flocks by night when angels appeared, according to Luke.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Myrrh: A resin from thorny Commiphora trees, used as perfume and in embalming; it is a gift often read as foreshadowing death.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Frankincense: A resin from Boswellia trees, burned as incense. It was traded across Arabia for millennia and prized almost like gold.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Santa Claus: The modern Santa is based on St. Nicholas, a fourth-century bishop, and shows up long after the stable.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Reindeer: Not at the stable; reindeer are Arctic animals, and they join Christmas through the 1823 poem about Santa.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Elf: Santa's workshop helpers are a modern invention, popularized in 1800s writing, not part of the nativity.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Snowman: Bethlehem hardly ever sees snow, though a rare storm dusted it in December 2013.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Rudolph: Rudolph's 1949 song, recorded by Gene Autry, became one of the best-selling Christmas records, but he's a modern addition.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Christmas tree: A German tradition. The nativity scene is older: St. Francis staged a living one at Greccio in 1223.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Stocking: Tied to the St. Nicholas legend, in which he tossed gold coins down a chimney into stockings drying by the fire.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Grinch: Dr. Seuss's grump from 1957. He has no place at the manger, and his heart only grows three sizes at the end.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Penguin: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, so none ever watched over any Bethlehem stable.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Mistletoe: A semi-parasitic plant with toxic berries. The kissing custom is English, and it has nothing to do with the nativity.
Things in a traditional nativity scene.Sleigh: Santa's ride. The word comes from the Dutch slee, and it has no place at the manger.

Hans Christian Andersen tales.The Little Mermaid: Published in 1837. In Andersen's version, the mermaid does not get the prince and dissolves into sea foam. A statue stands in Copenhagen harbor.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.The Ugly Duckling: Often read as semi-autobiographical: Andersen was a poor, awkward boy who rose to fame across Europe.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.The Snow Queen: From 1844, it inspired Disney's Frozen, though Andersen's story is far darker and takes seven parts.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Thumbelina: From 1835, she's a tiny girl born from a flower. Andersen called her "Little Tiny" in the title's Danish version.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Princess and the Pea: A 1835 story in which a pea under 20 mattresses proves a real princess. It's among Andersen's shortest.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Little Match Girl: A girl freezes to death on New Year's Eve while selling matches, an unflinching ending even for Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.The Red Shoes: A cursed pair of shoes dances a girl to exhaustion until she asks to have her feet cut off. The 1948 film made it famous.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.The Nightingale: The Emperor of China prefers a jeweled mechanical bird to a real nightingale. Some link the tale to Jenny Lind.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.The Fir Tree: A tree dreams of greatness, becomes a Christmas decoration, and is then tossed into the attic and burned.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Cinderella: A European folk tale known from Charles Perrault's 1697 version and the Grimms'. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Rapunzel: A Grimm tale, whose name comes from the rampion plant her mother craved. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Snow White: A Grimm fairy tale about a jealous queen, a poisoned apple and seven dwarfs. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Hansel and Gretel: A Grimm tale of two children, a witch and a gingerbread house, not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Rumpelstiltskin: A Grimm tale about a man whose name is guessed. Hans Christian Andersen didn't write it.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Sleeping Beauty: Told by Charles Perrault in 1697, and by the Grimms as Briar Rose. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Pinocchio: Carlo Collodi's Italian novel from 1883, about a wooden puppet. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie's 1904 play and 1911 novel. Not by Hans Christian Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Beauty and the Beast: A French tale first published in 1740 by Gabrielle-Suzanne de Villeneuve, later shortened. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Goldilocks: An English tale published by Robert Southey in 1837. It's not one of Andersen's.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Puss in Boots: Charles Perrault's 1697 fairy tale about a clever cat. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Frog Prince: A Grimm tale where a princess's kiss is replaced, in the original, by a throw against the wall.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Bluebeard: Charles Perrault's 1697 tale of a wealthy nobleman who has murdered his wives. Not Andersen.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Tom Thumb: An English tale first printed in the 1600s about a boy the size of a thumb, predating Andersen's own Thumbelina.
Hans Christian Andersen tales.Aladdin: An Arabian Nights story, popular worldwide, but not one of Andersen's.

Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Eye of newt: Newt is an amphibian, though in the play some scholars suspect old herb names may be hidden, such as mustard seed.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Toe of frog: Shakespeare's list pairs it with eye of newt: 'Eye of newt, and toe of frog'.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Wool of bat: Its rhyme partner is 'tongue of dog'. The bat's fur, called wool, is one of the strangest items in the brew.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Tongue of dog: Rhyming with 'wool of bat', this is one of the cauldron's odd animal parts.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Adder's fork: This refers to the forked tongue of a viper, the sort of venomous detail the witches love.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Blind-worm's sting: The blind-worm is a slow-worm, a legless lizard that is actually harmless and has no sting.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Lizard's leg: It appears in the same line as 'howlet's wing', a poetic word for an owl's wing.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Howlet's wing: A howlet is an owl, so this ingredient is owl's wing. The word is an old form of 'owlet'.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Scale of dragon: The brew includes the scale of dragon, a mythical creature, placed next to the tooth of wolf.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Tooth of wolf: Wolf's tooth follows dragon scale in the recipe, and then comes the witches' mummy.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Root of hemlock: Hemlock is the deadly poison that killed Socrates, and the witches say it must be dug up in the dark.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Gall of goat: This bitter bile comes near the end of the recipe, along with slips of yew cut during an eclipse.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Eye of frog: A trap: it is eye of newt and toe of frog in the play, so this swaps the two.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Toe of newt: A swap on the real line, which has the toe belong to the frog and the eye to the newt.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Wool of owl: The play has wool of bat, while owl appears in the form of howlet's wing.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Tongue of cat: The brew has tongue of dog, not cat. The cat in the play is Graymalkin, the witch's familiar.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Wing of bat: The bat contributes wool, not wing, in Shakespeare's verse. The wing belongs to the howlet.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Tail of rat: A rat appears elsewhere in the play, when a witch becomes a rat without a tail, but not in the brew.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Fang of snake: The snake's contribution is a 'fillet of a fenny snake', a slice of marsh snake, not a fang.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Leg of spider: Lizard supplies the leg in the actual list, so this one is invented.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Scale of snake: Dragon provides the scale in the real brew, and the snake gives a fillet.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Tooth of bear: Wolf provides the tooth in the recipe. Bears do not appear in the brew.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Heart of toad: Toad appears in the play's first cauldron lines as a creature that sweltered venom while it slept, but not as a heart.
Ingredients in the Macbeth witches' brew.Liver of raven: There is no raven in the brew, though a raven announces Duncan's death earlier in the play.
